newsitem.title: TAIWAN: No end in sight as Taiwan stocks hit six-year high.
newsitem.headline: No end in sight as Taiwan stocks hit six-year high.

text.p: Spurred by the improving economic outlook, Taiwan's stock market soared to a six-year high on Monday with analysts predicting no immediate end to the bull run that has seen the index gain more than 1,000 points in 1997.

Analysts said the market -- so positive that it turned last week's death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping into a rallying point -- may hit 8,500 points before April if recent expectations of an economic recovery play out to the fullest.

The index soared 168.67 points, or 2.18 percent, on Monday to close at 7,908.61, surpassing the 7,857.01 finish of June 2, 1990. It was the market's highest close since it ended at 7,927.17 on May 17, 1990.
At T$158.88 billion, the day's turnover was only slightly below Friday's sizzling three-year high of T$166.9 billion.
"The huge turnover means investors are extremely bullish about the market's outlook and are pouring their funds into this one market," said Nomura Securities economist Amy Huang.
"If Taiwan's economy lives up to expectations, the index is likely to hit 8,500 points by the end of the first quarter."

Hopes for a strong economy, which have helped add more than 1,000 points to the index since January, got another boost on Thursday with news that fourth-quarter gross domestic product grew a higher-than-expected 6.62 percent.

The result helped Taiwan's economy, which had slumped since mid-1995, record growth of 5.71 percent in 1996. It also led the government to raise its 1997 GDP forecast to 6.28 percent from 6.20 percent.
"Right now it is difficult to see when this bull run will end, as the market seems to ignore all technical resistance," said Wang Jieh, an analyst for Foremost Investment Services.

While analysts have warned that political instability in China in the wake of Deng's death could jeopardise Taiwan's increasingly China-dependent economy, Deng's demise has sparked the equivalent of a celebration rally on the island.

"Deng's death took out a lingering bearish factor," said Oliver Fang, senior analyst at National Securities. "Investors no longer have to worry about rumours on his health. In an already bullish market, the death turned out to be a boost."
Albert Lin, financial researcher at Golden Securities, said the near-term market focus would fall on fundamentals-backed sectors such as plastics, textiles and electronics.
"The market's future gains will reflect pure economic factors and, therefore, firms with strong fundamentals are the ones that will benefit," Lin said.

Nomura's Huang said the Taiwan dollar's resilience in the face of the U.S. dollar's prolonged rise, and its resulting strength against the yen and other currencies, had not had a significant impact on inflows of foreign funds for the bullish stock market.
"The fact is, Taiwan's stock market right now is one of the very best in Asia to invest in, so foreign funds are coming regardless of how the rates are going," Huang said.
Statistics from the Securities and Exchange Commission showed that foreigners poured a net T$5.757 billion (US$209 million) into Taiwan shares in February alone.
But National's Fang said the market's bull run had been fuelled mostly by domestic investors, since foreign holdings still comprise less than five percent of market capitalisation.
"While foreign investments have been growing, domestic investments are growing even faster," he said.
